steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Satellites orbit Earth for communications, navigation, weather forecasting, Earth observation and scientific research

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Geostationary orbit: 35,786 km above the equator, 24-hour period, satellite appears stationary — used for comms and weather

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Low Earth orbit (LEO): 160–2,000 km, ~90-minute period — used for Earth observation and the ISS

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Polar orbit: passes over the poles, allowing full Earth coverage — used for mapping and reconnaissance

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What are the advantages of a geostationary orbit? | Q: Why are polar orbits useful for Earth observation? | Q: Name three types of space probe and their functions.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: The satellite remains above the same point on Earth, so ground antennas don't need to track it. Ideal for communications and weather monitoring of a fixed region. | The satellite passes over different parts of Earth on each orbit as the planet rotates beneath it, eventually covering the entire surface — ideal for mapping and environmental monitoring. | Orbiter: orbits a body for long-term remote study (e.g. Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter). Lander: touches down to study the surface in situ (e.g. Philae). Rover: a mobile lander that can explore multiple

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Geostationary: 35,786 km, equator, 24-hour period — know all three criteria Compare GEO vs LEO: GEO = fixed coverage, LEO = global coverage over time Both boards test satellite orbits and their applications Kessler syndrome is on the Edexcel specification — understand the concept
